summary: The article surveys ancient crafts across cultures, including textiles, ceramics, metalwork, woodworking, glassblowing and rug making, showing how artisans keep these traditions alive despite industrialization and mass production. Each craft is tied to named practitioners and to the history, identity and values of its community. It concludes that these crafts are living embodiments of enduring values and cultural memory in an increasingly homogenized world.
one_line: A comparative tour of textile, ceramic, metal, wood, glass and rug crafts worldwide, showing how artisans preserve cultural identity and heritage.
key_facts: A nationwide movement to revive handloom weaving in India began around September 7, 2023, pioneered by textile historian Aarav Mehta and social entrepreneur Preeti Singh.
Indian textiles celebrated for regional identity include the handloom weaves of Varanasi, the cotton dhurries of Rajasthan, and the silks of Assam.
Martina Quispe, an indigenous craftsperson from the highlands of Peru, said on October 20, 2023 that each pattern in her textiles tells part of her community's history and cosmology.

Chinese porcelain, known as 'White Gold,' dates back to the Eastern Han Dynasty; master potter Jian Wei of Jingdezhen described the craft on November 15, 2023 as a philosophical journey uniting earth, water and fire.
Greek artisan Elena Votsi preserves red-figure and black-figure pottery techniques, drawing on ancient epics and battles to illustrate vases and urns.
Bronze casting in Benin dates back to the 13th century; artisan Yawo Agboka, from a guild that worked for the Benin royal court, spoke about it on September 17, 2023.
Masaru Emoto, a bladesmith from the Chūbu region, said on December 3, 2023 that each Japanese sword is a 'soul of the samurai' reflecting the code of Bushido.
Nigerian carpenter Emeka Okafor showcased intricate relief carvings of ancestral stories and daily activities on October 30, 2023.
Scandinavian wood carving harks back to the Viking Age; artisans like Ingrid Svensson draw on Norse mythology and seafaring tradition.
Murano glassblowing in Italy, with artisans like Luca Amato, has existed since the 8th century, while Middle Eastern glassblowing began around the 1st century B.C.
Persian rugs trace back to the 5th century B.C.; Farzaneh Hosseini of Shiraz said on October 12, 2023 that each rug is a testament to her ancestors' art.
Kyrgyz master weaver Ainura Serikova noted on September 25, 2023 that Kyrgyz rugs are entwined with the nomadic lifestyle and reflect landscape and seasons.
